title: Interpret a rare positive alarm
scope: One binary observation with specified sensitivity and false-positive rate

items.prompt: 1% of motors in a fleet have a bearing fault. The vibration alarm fires for 99% of faulty motors (sensitivity) and for 3% of healthy motors (false-positive rate). One motor's alarm fires once. Compute P(fault | alarm) as a probability, not a percentage. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
items.solution: Fault-and-alarm = 0.01·0.99 = 0.0099. Healthy-and-alarm = 0.99·0.03 = 0.0297. P(alarm) = 0.0099 + 0.0297 = 0.0396. P(fault | alarm) = 0.0099/0.0396 = 0.25. The sensitivity 0.99 alone is not the posterior.
hints: You want P(fault | alarm), not P(alarm | fault). Alarms come from faulty motors and from healthy ones.
Compute the two ways an alarm happens: fault-and-alarm = 0.01·0.99 and healthy-and-alarm = 0.99·0.03. The posterior is the fault share of their sum.

Fault-and-alarm = 0.01·0.99 = 0.0099. Healthy-and-alarm = 0.99·0.03 = 0.0297. P(alarm) = 0.0099 + 0.0297 = 0.0396. P(fault | alarm) = 0.0099/0.0396 = 0.25. The sensitivity 0.99 alone is not the posterior.
items.remediation: 0.99 is the sensitivity P(alarm | fault), not the posterior. If you got about 0.248 you used 0.03 instead of 0.99·0.03 for the healthy-and-alarm term. Revisit /lessons/M08.

items.prompt: 4% of gearboxes leaving a line are faulty. An acoustic check has sensitivity 80% and specificity 95% (it stays silent for 95% of good gearboxes). The check flags one gearbox. Compute P(faulty | flag) as a probability. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
hints: Specificity is P(no flag | good). The false-positive rate P(flag | good) is 1 minus the specificity.
Convert specificity 95% into a false-positive rate, then compute faulty-and-flag = 0.04·0.8 and good-and-flag = 0.96·(that rate).
items.remediation: If you got about 0.034 you used the specificity 0.95 as the false-positive rate. If you got 0.8 you reported the sensitivity. Revisit /lessons/M08.

items.prompt: 1 in 100 battery packs has a cell defect. A thermal screen misses 10% of defective packs (false-negative rate) and has specificity 98% on good packs. One pack is flagged. Compute P(defect | flag) as a probability. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
hints: Both rates are stated the other way round: convert the miss rate into a sensitivity and the specificity into a false-positive rate first.
Sensitivity = 1 - miss rate and false-positive rate = 1 - specificity. Then form defect-and-flag (0.01 times the sensitivity) and good-and-flag (0.99 times the false-positive rate).
items.remediation: If you got about 0.048 you used the miss rate 0.10 as the sensitivity. If you got about 0.0092 you used the specificity 0.98 as the false-positive rate. Revisit /lessons/M08.

items.prompt: An expected-count table for 10000 screened parts: 400 defective parts (360 test positive, 40 negative) and 9600 good parts (240 test positive, 9360 negative). A part tests positive. Compute P(defective | positive) as a probability. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
items.solution: Positives = 360 + 240 = 600. P(defective | positive) = 360/600 = 0.6. Dividing 360 by all 10000 parts or by the 400 defective parts answers a different question.
hints: Given a positive result, only the positive column of the table matters.
Add the two positive cells (defective-positive and good-positive) to get all positives; the posterior is the defective share of that total.
Positives = 360 + 240 = 600. P(defective | positive) = 360/600 = 0.6. Dividing 360 by all 10000 parts or by the 400 defective parts answers a different question.
items.remediation: 0.9 is the sensitivity (360/400) and 0.036 is P(defective and positive) (360/10000); neither conditions on the positive result. Revisit /lessons/M08.

items.prompt: A batch of 2000 castings has 8% porosity defects. An X-ray screen flags 85% of defective castings and 10% of good castings. Build the expected-count table and compute P(defective | flagged) as a probability. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
items.solution: Defective = 0.08·2000 = 160 and good = 1840. Flagged-defective = 0.85·160 = 136; flagged-good = 0.10·1840 = 184. P(defective | flagged) = 136/(136 + 184) = 136/320 = 0.425.
hints: Build the table first: split the batch into defective and good rows, then split each row into flagged and not flagged.
Defective = 8% of 2000 and good = the rest. Flagged-defective = 85% of the defective row and flagged-good = 10% of the good row; then condition on the flagged column.
Defective = 0.08·2000 = 160 and good = 1840. Flagged-defective = 0.85·160 = 136; flagged-good = 0.10·1840 = 184. P(defective | flagged) = 136/(136 + 184) = 136/320 = 0.425.
items.remediation: If you got about 0.405 you took 10% of all 2000 castings (200) as false positives; the 10% applies only to the 1840 good castings. Revisit /lessons/M08.

items.prompt: A screening report for 8000 valves lists only the negatives: of 200 leaking valves, 20 tested negative; of 7800 sound valves, 7020 tested negative. A valve tests positive. Compute P(leaking | positive) as a probability. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
items.solution: Positive-leaking = 180 and positive-sound = 780, so positives = 960. P(leaking | positive) = 180/960 = 0.1875 (= 3/16).
hints: The report gives the negative cells; recover the positive cells by subtraction before conditioning.
Positive-leaking = 200 - 20 and positive-sound = 7800 - 7020. Then use only the positive column.
Positive-leaking = 180 and positive-sound = 780, so positives = 960. P(leaking | positive) = 180/960 = 0.1875 (= 3/16).
items.remediation: If you got about 0.003 you used the negative column (20/7040), which is P(leaking | negative). If you got 0.9 you reported the sensitivity 180/200. Revisit /lessons/M08.
